articles.title: Hidden charcoal reveals the true age of ancient cave paintings
articles.summary: A new analysis has precisely dated paintings in France’s Font-de-Gaume cave for the first time. Scientists discovered charcoal inside black pigments once thought to contain only minerals, allowing them to use radiocarbon dating. The results show that a bison was painted about 13,000 years ago, while sections of a mask-like figure were added during several widely separated periods.
articles.content:
For the first time, scientists have accurately determined the age of prehistoric paintings inside Font-de-Gaume, a celebrated decorated cave near Les Eyzies in Dordogne (southwestern France).

The new findings provide firm dates for two black images, a bison and a masklike figure, and reveal that parts of the artwork were created during widely separated periods. The results could give archaeologists a powerful new way to reconstruct when people entered decorated caves, made paintings, and returned to alter or add to them.

Why Ice Age Cave Paintings Are Difficult to Date

Dordogne is home to some of the best-known prehistoric art in Europe, including the paintings at Lascaux. Yet determining exactly when many of these images were created has remained extremely difficult.

Radiocarbon dating works by measuring carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon that gradually disappears after an organism dies. Because charcoal is made from burned organic material, it can often be dated using this method. Mineral pigments, however, usually contain no carbon and therefore cannot be analyzed in the same way.

Researchers had long believed that many black paintings in the region were made entirely from iron and manganese oxides. These naturally occurring minerals can produce dark pigments, but they do not contain the organic carbon needed for radiocarbon dating.

As a result, the artwork was generally considered impossible to date directly. However, scientists had never conclusively demonstrated that the pigments contained no carbon at all.

Searching for Charcoal Hidden in the Pigment

To investigate, the researchers analyzed the chemical composition of two black figures at Font-de-Gaume. One depicts a bison, while the other is commonly described as a mask.

The team used Raman microspectrometry and hyperspectral imaging, two techniques that can identify materials without noticeably damaging the artwork.

Raman microspectrometry uses light to examine how molecules vibrate, producing a chemical signature that can help identify pigments and other substances. Hyperspectral imaging records subtle differences in color and reflected light at each point in an image. Scientists can use those measurements to determine which compounds are present.

Hyperspectral imaging is widely used in cultural heritage research because it can reveal features that are difficult or impossible to see with the human eye. It also has applications in biomedical science, agriculture, environmental monitoring, and astrophysics.

Both methods revealed traces of charcoal in the paintings' black pigment.

The charcoal was distributed consistently throughout the black lines of the figures. That pattern was important because it indicated that the carbon was part of the original pigment rather than contamination left by later graffiti, visitors, or tourist activity inside the cave.

Tiny Samples Reveal the Paintings' Ages

Once the charcoal had been confirmed, researchers received exceptional authorization to remove extremely small samples for carbon-14 dating.

Analyzing such limited material is technically challenging. Scientists must collect enough carbon to obtain a reliable measurement while removing as little as possible from the ancient image.

The results confirmed that the bison dates to the Upper Paleolithic, the later portion of the Old Stone Age when anatomically modern humans created many of Europe's most famous cave paintings.

The bison was painted between 13,461 and 13,162 calBP.

CalBP means Calibrated Before Present, with present conventionally defined as the year 1950. Radiocarbon measurements must be calibrated because the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has changed over time. Those variations can be influenced by factors including solar activity and changes in Earth's magnetic field.

The new date places the bison slightly later than previous estimates.

A Mysterious Mask Created Across Different Periods

The mask produced an even more complex result. Samples from separate parts of the figure yielded three different ranges.

One section was dated to between 8,993 and 8,590 calBP. Another was dated to between 15,981 and 15,121 calBP, while a third was placed between 15,297 and 14,246 calBP.

These results suggest that the image may contain elements created at very different times. Rather than being the work of a single artist during one visit, the mask may preserve multiple episodes of artistic activity separated by thousands of years.

That possibility offers a more layered picture of prehistoric cave art. Decorated caves may not always have been completed during a single period. Some could have remained meaningful places that later communities revisited, modified, or reinterpreted.

A New Tool for Understanding Prehistoric Art

The research was led by a scientist from the Laboratoire de développement instrumental et de méthodologies innovantes pour les biens culturels (Chimie ParisTech-PSL/CNRS/Ministère de la Culture). The study was published in PNAS.

The research brought together specialists from several French scientific and cultural institutions.

Contributors included scientists from Laboratoire de mesure du carbone 14 (CEA/CNRS/IRD/ASNR/ Ministère de la Culture), a national platform affiliated with Laboratoire des sciences du climat et de l'environnement (CEA/CNRS/ Université de Versailles Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines). Researchers from the Histoire naturelle des Humanités préhistoriques laboratory (CNRS/MNHN/Université de Perpignan Via Domitia), the Centre des monuments nationaux, and the Centre de recherche et de restauration des musées de France also participated.

By combining chemical imaging with highly sensitive radiocarbon measurements, the team has developed a method that could be applied to other prehistoric figures previously considered undatable.

More precise dates could help researchers determine which paintings were created during the same period, how artistic styles changed, and whether generations of people repeatedly returned to particular caves. That information may ultimately reveal more about the communities that produced the images and the cultural importance these underground spaces held over thousands of years.

articles.personality_title: Scientists accurately date ancient cave paintings using hidden charcoal
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long struggled to find exact dates for prehistoric cave paintings because many black pigments contain minerals without carbon, making radiocarbon dating impossible. The Font-de-Gaume cave in southwestern France has famous paintings, but their ages were uncertain.

**What happened** – Researchers discovered tiny amounts of charcoal inside the black pigments of two paintings in Font-de-Gaume: a bison and a mask-like figure. Using special imaging techniques, they confirmed the presence of charcoal, which allowed them to use radiocarbon dating for the first time on these artworks. The bison was dated to about 13,000 years ago. The mask showed parts painted during three different time periods, some separated by thousands of years.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it provides a new way to date ancient cave paintings directly, rather than relying on indirect clues. It also shows that some artwork was created over long periods, suggesting caves were revisited and modified by different groups. This helps archaeologists better understand how prehistoric people interacted with these sites.

**What's next step** – Scientists hope to use this method on other caves with black paintings thought to be undatable. More precise dating can reveal patterns in when and how prehistoric art was made, showing changes in styles and how communities returned to these caves over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Finding charcoal hidden in cave painting pigments has allowed scientists to date ancient artworks accurately, revealing new insights into prehistoric human culture and cave use over thousands of years.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques datent avec précision des peintures rupestres anciennes grâce au charbon caché
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques ont longtemps eu du mal à dater précisément les peintures rupestres parce que beaucoup de pigments noirs contiennent des minéraux sans carbone, rendant la datation au radiocarbone impossible. La grotte de Font-de-Gaume en France, célèbre pour ses peintures, avait des âges incertains.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont découvert de minuscules traces de charbon dans les pigments noirs de deux peintures de Font-de-Gaume : un bison et une figure ressemblant à un masque. Grâce à des techniques d'imagerie spéciales, ils ont confirmé la présence de charbon, ce qui leur a permis d'utiliser pour la première fois la datation au radiocarbone sur ces œuvres. Le bison a été daté d'environ 13 000 ans. Le masque montre des parties peintes à trois périodes différentes, séparées par des milliers d'années.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle offre une nouvelle méthode pour dater directement les peintures anciennes, plutôt que de se baser sur des indices indirects. Elle montre aussi que certaines œuvres ont été créées sur de longues périodes, suggérant que les grottes ont été revisitées et modifiées par différents groupes. Cela aide les archéologues à mieux comprendre l’usage de ces sites par les hommes préhistoriques.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques espèrent appliquer cette méthode à d’autres grottes avec des peintures noires considérées comme impossibles à dater. Des datations plus précises pourront révéler les moments et les façons dont l’art préhistorique a été créé, montrant les changements de styles et les retours des communautés dans ces grottes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La découverte de charbon caché dans les pigments des peintures rupestres a permis aux scientifiques de dater précisément ces œuvres anciennes, offrant de nouvelles connaissances sur la culture préhistorique et l’utilisation des grottes sur des milliers d’années.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos datan con precisión pinturas rupestres antiguas usando carbón oculto
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos han tenido dificultades para fechar con exactitud las pinturas rupestres porque muchos pigmentos negros contienen minerales sin carbono, lo que impide usar la datación por radiocarbono. La cueva Font-de-Gaume en el suroeste de Francia tiene pinturas famosas, pero sus edades eran inciertas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores encontraron pequeñas cantidades de carbón dentro de los pigmentos negros de dos pinturas en Font-de-Gaume: un bisonte y una figura parecida a una máscara. Usando técnicas especiales de imagen, confirmaron la presencia de carbón, lo que les permitió usar la datación por radiocarbono por primera vez en estas obras. El bisonte fue fechado en unos 13,000 años. La máscara mostró partes pintadas en tres períodos diferentes, separados por miles de años.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque ofrece una nueva forma de fechar directamente pinturas rupestres antiguas, en lugar de depender de pistas indirectas. También muestra que algunas obras se realizaron durante largos períodos, lo que sugiere que las cuevas fueron visitadas y modificadas por diferentes grupos. Esto ayuda a los arqueólogos a entender mejor cómo la gente prehistórica usaba estos sitios.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos esperan usar este método en otras cuevas con pinturas negras que se creían imposibles de fechar. Fechas más precisas pueden mostrar patrones de cuándo y cómo se hizo el arte prehistórico, revelando cambios en estilos y cómo las comunidades regresaron a estas cuevas con el tiempo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Encontrar carbón oculto en los pigmentos de las pinturas rupestres permitió a los científicos fechar con precisión estas antiguas obras, revelando nuevas ideas sobre la cultura humana prehistórica y el uso de cuevas durante miles de años.

articles.title: Mount Olympus and D-Day beaches among new World Heritage Sites
articles.summary: From the peaks of Mount Olympus in Greece to the shores of the “D-Day” beaches in France, 25 cultural or natural landmarks from across the globe have been newly inscribed on the World Heritage List, updated annually by the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).
articles.content:
The announcement on Tuesday came during the World Heritage Committee’s meeting in Busan, Republic of Korea, being held from 19 to 29 July.

The List includes first-time inscriptions from three African countries: Comoros, São Tomé and Príncipe, and South Sudan.

Tweet URL

Here are a few of the sites “considered to be of outstanding value to humanity”:

Mount Olympus, Greece

The wider area of Mount Olympus – Greece’s highest mountain and the mythical home of Zeus and other ancient gods – was added to the UN list.

Situated in the country’s north, the mountain is an enduring emblem of Greek civilisation.

UNESCO said its proximity to the sea and abrupt elevation produces a remarkable diversity in terrain, climate and vegetation.

The property features striking landforms, including limestone cliffs, karstic sinkholes and cirques, which are bowl-shaped amphitheatre-like valleys carved by glacial erosion.

D-Day beaches, France

Six sites associated with the Allied forces landings in Normandy, France, on 6 June 1944 – marking a major turning point in the Second World War – also were recognised.

The five “D-Day” beaches and Point du Hoc stretch along roughly 80 km of coastline. From there, hundreds of thousands of American, British and Canadian troops launched one of the largest military operations ever, ultimately liberating Western Europe and defeating Nazi Germany.

UNESCO noted that the property preserves significant remains of the German Atlantic wall alongside battlefield traces and original wartime equipment as well as commemorative landscapes such as the American Cemetery at Colleville‑sur‑Mer.

“Together, these elements form an exceptional cultural landscape shaped both by the events of 1944 and by their enduring remembrance,” the agency said.

ONU News/ Felipe de Carvalho

Amazonia theatres, Brazil

Two theatres in Brazil’s Amazon region are now on the World Heritage List.

The Theatro da Paz in the city of Belém and Teatro Amazonas in Manaus were built during the so-called Amazonian “Golden Age”, which resulted from the period of economic prosperity known as the Rubber Cycle, between 1879 and 1912.

The buildings were inspired by European architecture, particularly French, and are decorated with Amazonian motifs. They were “designed as symbols of political and urban ambition”.

The Theatro da Paz, in the historic centre of Belém in Pará, was inaugurated in 1878. It is part of developments that highlighted the strategic role of the city as a port and state capital in addition to celebrating the recently founded Brazilian Republic.

The Amazonas Theatre opened its doors in 1896 and marked part of a large-scale urban development in Manaus, symbolising the wealth and prestige of the future capital of the Amazon.

articles.personality_title: Mount Olympus and D-Day beaches join UNESCO World Heritage List
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year, UNESCO, the United Nations group that protects important places around the world, adds new sites to its World Heritage List. These sites are special because they have cultural, historical, or natural value that is important for all people.

**What happened** – In July 2023, UNESCO added 25 new places to the World Heritage List. Among them are Mount Olympus in Greece, famous as the home of ancient Greek gods, and the D-Day beaches in France, where a key battle of World War II took place. Other new sites include two theatres in Brazil’s Amazon region and first-time listings from three African countries: Comoros, São Tomé and Príncipe, and South Sudan.

**Impact** – Adding these sites helps protect and remember important parts of history and nature. For example, Mount Olympus is not only a mountain but also a symbol of Greek culture with unique landscapes. The D-Day beaches preserve the memory of a major World War II event, including old military remains and cemeteries. The Amazon theatres show the rich cultural history of Brazil’s Amazon during a time of growth and wealth.

**What’s next step** – Now that these places are on the World Heritage List, they will receive more attention and support to keep them safe and well-preserved. This means future generations can learn from and enjoy these special sites. Countries will also work together to protect these places and share their stories with the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UNESCO’s addition of Mount Olympus, D-Day beaches, and other sites highlights the importance of protecting diverse cultural and natural landmarks worldwide for future generations.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le mont Olympe et les plages du Débarquement inscrits au patrimoine mondial de l’UNESCO
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, l’UNESCO, l’organisation des Nations Unies qui protège les lieux importants dans le monde, ajoute de nouveaux sites à sa liste du patrimoine mondial. Ces sites sont spéciaux car ils ont une valeur culturelle, historique ou naturelle importante pour tous.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En juillet 2023, l’UNESCO a inscrit 25 nouveaux sites sur la liste du patrimoine mondial. Parmi eux, le mont Olympe en Grèce, célèbre comme la maison des dieux grecs anciens, et les plages du Débarquement en France, où une bataille clé de la Seconde Guerre mondiale a eu lieu. D’autres sites nouveaux incluent deux théâtres dans la région amazonienne du Brésil et des inscriptions pour la première fois de trois pays africains : Comores, Sao Tomé-et-Principe et Soudan du Sud.

**Impact** – Inscrire ces sites aide à protéger et à se souvenir de parties importantes de l’histoire et de la nature. Par exemple, le mont Olympe n’est pas seulement une montagne mais aussi un symbole de la culture grecque avec des paysages uniques. Les plages du Débarquement gardent la mémoire d’un événement majeur de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, avec des vestiges militaires et des cimetières. Les théâtres amazoniens montrent l’histoire culturelle riche de l’Amazonie brésilienne pendant une période de croissance.

**Prochaine étape** – Maintenant que ces lieux sont inscrits au patrimoine mondial, ils recevront plus d’attention et de soutien pour rester protégés et bien conservés. Cela permettra aux générations futures d’apprendre et de profiter de ces sites spéciaux. Les pays travailleront aussi ensemble pour protéger ces endroits et partager leurs histoires.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’inscription par l’UNESCO du mont Olympe, des plages du Débarquement et d’autres sites montre l’importance de préserver des lieux culturels et naturels variés dans le monde pour les générations à venir.
articles.personality_title_es: El monte Olimpo y las playas del Día D se suman a la lista de Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, la UNESCO, el grupo de Naciones Unidas que protege lugares importantes en el mundo, añade nuevos sitios a su Lista del Patrimonio Mundial. Estos sitios son especiales porque tienen valor cultural, histórico o natural importante para todas las personas.

**Qué pasó** – En julio de 2023, la UNESCO añadió 25 nuevos lugares a la Lista del Patrimonio Mundial. Entre ellos están el monte Olimpo en Grecia, famoso como la casa de los dioses griegos antiguos, y las playas del Día D en Francia, donde tuvo lugar una batalla clave de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Otros sitios nuevos incluyen dos teatros en la región amazónica de Brasil y primeras inscripciones de tres países africanos: Comoras, Santo Tomé y Príncipe, y Sudán del Sur.

**Impacto** – Añadir estos sitios ayuda a proteger y recordar partes importantes de la historia y la naturaleza. Por ejemplo, el monte Olimpo no es solo una montaña, sino también un símbolo de la cultura griega con paisajes únicos. Las playas del Día D conservan la memoria de un evento importante de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, con restos militares y cementerios. Los teatros amazónicos muestran la rica historia cultural de la Amazonía brasileña durante un tiempo de crecimiento.

**Próximo paso** – Ahora que estos lugares están en la Lista del Patrimonio Mundial, recibirán más atención y apoyo para mantenerse seguros y bien conservados. Esto permitirá que las futuras generaciones aprendan y disfruten de estos sitios especiales. Los países también trabajarán juntos para proteger estos lugares y compartir sus historias con el mundo.

**Resumen en una frase** – La inclusión del monte Olimpo, las playas del Día D y otros sitios por parte de la UNESCO destaca la importancia de proteger lugares culturales y naturales diversos en todo el mundo para las futuras generaciones.
